passage: At the village school near Udaipur, teacher Uday asked the class, "Who can tell me what a seed needs?" Pallavi, five, looked at her desk. Nobody spoke. Uday leaned back against the table and counted silently to five. Pallavi's fingers curled. Then very softly she said, "Water." "Yes, water," said Uday. "What else?" Silence again, and he waited. "The sun," she said. The girl next to her said, "And soil!" Uday smiled. He had not repeated the question once.

qa.q: What did Uday ask the class?
qa.a: He asked, "Who can tell me what a seed needs?"

qa.q: What might Pallavi's silence after the question suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It may have meant she was thinking or feeling shy, since she looked at her desk and then answered softly. She might also not have understood the question.

qa.q: What did Uday do that gave Pallavi room to answer?
qa.a: He counted silently to five and waited without rephrasing, and did the same again for her next answer.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Uday waits and does not rush her?
qa.a: She may feel calmer and more able to speak, because no one is pressuring her.

grounding: A preschooler learns that conversation involves waiting, and a wise adult counts to five before rephrasing.

passage: In a Ankara kindergarten, teacher Pablo asked, "What is your favourite colour, Zeynep?" Zeynep, five, looked at the floor and said nothing. Pablo counted slowly in his head: one, two, three, four, five. Zeynep swung her foot. He smiled but did not repeat the question. Then she whispered, "Yellow." "Yellow! Like the sun?" She nodded. "Why?" After another pause, she said, "It looks warm." Pablo said, "I liked waiting for that answer."

qa.q: What colour did Zeynep name?
qa.a: She named yellow.

qa.q: What might Zeynep's silence have meant, and what does her answer suggest?
qa.a: She may have been thinking or shy. Her answer that yellow "looks warm" suggests she had a thoughtful reason all along.

qa.q: What could Pablo do if Zeynep still did not answer after a count of five?
qa.a: He can rephrase kindly or offer a choice, since silence may also mean she did not understand.

qa.q: How might Zeynep feel when Pablo says he liked waiting for her answer?
qa.a: She may feel valued and safe, and more willing to speak next time.

grounding: A preschooler learns that conversation involves waiting, and a wise adult counts to five before rephrasing.

passage: At circle time in the nursery, Jasleen Ma'am asked, “Tejas, what did you have for breakfast?” Tejas looked at her and said nothing. The silence felt long. Jasleen didn't repeat the question. She counted to five in her head, smiling. One… two… three… four… On five, Tejas said, “Paratha. With pickle.” “Yum,” said Jasleen. Later she asked him another question and waited again. This time he answered on three, and then asked her, “What did you eat?”

qa.q: What did Tejas have for breakfast?
qa.a: Paratha, with pickle.

qa.q: What might Tejas's silence have meant?
qa.a: He may have been thinking, or feeling shy in front of the circle. Once he had time, he felt comfortable enough to answer and even ask a question back.

qa.q: Why was counting to five a good idea?
qa.a: It gave Tejas time to think without pressure, instead of rushing to repeat or rephrase the question.

qa.q: How might the other children see the long pause?
qa.a: They might learn that waiting is part of a conversation, and that it's okay to take time to answer.

grounding: A teacher waits by counting to five after asking a preschooler a question, giving him time to think and answer.

passage: I'm Uma, the receptionist at the clinic. Today the doctor asked Kishore, “Where does it hurt?” Kishore stared at her. After one second, she asked again, “Is it your tummy? Your head? Your ear?” Kishore looked even more confused. His mother touched the doctor's arm. “He needs a little time.” They waited. Kishore finally pointed to his ear. “Here. It goes buzz.” I'm not sure if he was shy or just didn't understand, but waiting got the answer.

qa.q: Where did Kishore point?
qa.a: To his ear.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when he looked even more confused?
qa.a: He was probably confused and overwhelmed by too many questions too quickly, or shy with the doctor. Uma couldn't tell which.

qa.q: What would you advise the doctor next time a child goes silent?
qa.a: Wait a few seconds, maybe counting to five, before rephrasing, so the child has time to think.

qa.q: How did Kishore's mother see the situation?
qa.a: She knew he needed time to answer, so she asked the doctor to wait.

grounding: A clinic receptionist observes that waiting after a question works better than rushing to rephrase for a silent child.

passage:
Monday: Omkar asked Sabina, “What was the best part of your day?” Silence. He answered for her: “The swings, I bet.” Sabina shrugged.
Wednesday: Omkar asked again and counted to five in his head. On four, Sabina said, “The ladybird on my hand.”
Friday: Omkar asked, “What was the best part?” Sabina thought, then said, “Painting.” Then she asked him, “What was your best part, Papa?” and waited, counting on her fingers. He laughed. “This part.”

qa.q: What was the best part of Sabina's day on Wednesday?
qa.a: The ladybird on her hand.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she shrugged on Monday?
qa.a: She was probably a little disappointed or unheard, since her father answered for her before she could think.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Omkar counted to five before speaking, giving Sabina time to think of her own answer.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Sabina waits for his answer on her fingers?
qa.a: He likely feels touched and amused that she learned to wait in turn, which is why he laughs.

grounding: Over a week, a father learns to count to five after asking a question, and his preschooler learns turn-taking and waiting.

passage:
The queue at the ice-cream cart was long and the vendor was already looking impatient. Lalit Mama crouched next to Gopika. "Which flavour, mango or chocolate?"

Gopika stared at the pictures. Silence.

The man behind them sighed. Lalit Mama counted to five in his head and waited.

"Mango," she said.

"Cone or cup?" asked the vendor.

Gopika said nothing again, looking lost. Lalit Mama counted to five, then pointed. "This crunchy one, or this little bowl?"

"Crunchy one!"

qa.q: Which flavour did Gopika choose?
qa.a: Mango.

qa.q: What does Gopika's second silence suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was probably confused, because she didn't understand "cone or cup"; she looked lost. Her first silence was more likely her thinking, or feeling shy with a queue watching.

qa.q: What did Lalit Mama do that helped Gopika answer?
qa.a: He counted to five before speaking again, and when she still didn't answer, he rephrased the question by pointing to the crunchy one and the bowl.

qa.q: How does the man behind them see the pause?
qa.a: He finds it slow and sighs, not knowing Gopika needs time to think and understand.

grounding: It shows a preschooler going silent after questions, from thinking or not understanding, and an adult counting to five before rephrasing.
